claims.text: The starting material is a magnetic high-entropy alloy in an as-solidified, disordered state.
Isothermal annealing of the as-solidified alloy will produce nanoscale precipitates.
The annealing-induced nanoscale precipitates will be homogeneously dispersed.
Nanoscale precipitates will act as domain-wall pinning sites.
Pinning by the precipitates will impede domain-wall motion.
Impeded domain-wall motion will increase the coercive field.
The annealed alloy will have a higher coercive field than the composition-matched as-solidified alloy.
The proposed intervention is annealing at approximately 600°C for one hour under an inert atmosphere, followed by rapid quenching.
The predicted coercivity increase is expected at ambient measurement temperature below the alloy's Curie temperature under standardized magnetic-field cycling.
Composition and annealing temperature can alter phase decomposition and its characteristic length scale in high-entropy alloys.
The coercivity effect may change when alloy composition or thermal-processing parameters deviate from the proposed conditions.
The optimal annealing duration and cooling rate for maximizing precipitate formation without detrimental effects are not known precisely.
No quantitative magnitude of the expected coercivity increase is predicted.
Failure to observe a statistically significant coercivity increase in the annealed samples relative to the untreated controls would falsify the hypothesis.
Absence of the expected homogeneous nanoscale precipitate dispersion would falsify the hypothesis.
